Recurrent Networks: Forecasting the Weather in Chachapoyas

Step 1: memory by hand · Step 2: data and task · Step 3: baselines · Step 4: train an LSTM · Step 5: predictions
A CNN re-uses the same small filter at every position of an image. A recurrent neural network (RNN) re-uses the same small network at every step of a sequence: hour after hour of weather, day after day of sensor readings, or letter after letter of DNA. While it reads, it keeps a running summary of what it has seen so far, called the hidden state. In this notebook we will build intuition for the hidden state, then train an RNN (an LSTM) to forecast the temperature in Chachapoyas, and always compare it with simple baselines.

Step 1: Memory by hand

An RNN keeps a running memory, its hidden state, updated every hour from the new input and the previous state.
Think of soil moisture. It goes up when it rains and slowly dries out afterwards, so it "remembers" past rain. We can write this as a tiny RNN with a single neuron: new state = r × previous state + rain this hour The number r controls the memory: with r = 0 the state only reflects the current hour; with r close to 1 it remembers rain from days ago. The same rule, with the same numbers, is applied every hour: this is weight sharing across time, just as a CNN shares its filter across space. A real RNN works the same way, but it has many hidden units instead of one, adds a non-linear activation, and learns its numbers from data instead of us choosing them.

Step 2: The data and the forecasting task

Hourly weather for Chachapoyas (2023–2024). Task: predict a value F hours ahead from the last H hours.
The data comes from NASA POWER, a free service that estimates hourly weather for any point on Earth from satellites and weather models. It is not a weather station: each value represents an area of roughly 50 km around Chachapoyas, so local effects (valleys, slopes) are smoothed out. The notebook can use a real station series instead (a CSV with a time column and columns such as temperature, humidity and rainfall).
With time series we never shuffle before splitting: the model must be tested on a period that comes after everything it learned from, as in real forecasting. We use the first 70% of the record (January 2023 to late May 2024) for training, the next 15% (June to mid-September 2024) for validation, and the last 15% (mid-September to December 2024) as the test period. Each variable is rescaled using the mean and spread of the training period only.

Step 3: Baselines first

Before any neural network: how good are the simplest possible guesses?
  • Persistence: "in F hours it will be the same as now".
  • Same hour yesterday: "in F hours it will be the same as at that hour yesterday". This uses the strong daily cycle of temperature and humidity in Chachapoyas.
A model is only useful if it beats these free guesses on the test period. The error is the mean absolute error (MAE): the average size of the mistake, in °C or %.

Step 4: Train an LSTM

An LSTM is an RNN with gates that decide what to keep, what to add and what to report.
A plain RNN tends to forget: information from many hours ago fades away as it is mixed into the hidden state again and again. An LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) adds a separate long-term memory and three learned gates:
  • Forget gate: what to erase from memory (for example, yesterday's rain once the soil dried).
  • Input gate: what new information to store.
  • Output gate: what part of the memory to use for the current output.
The gates give the network a choice about what to remember, instead of forgetting by default.

data.text/markdown: Estimated training time: about 10 s

data.text/html:
The network we train, unrolled over the input hours (updates with the settings above and in Step 2):
There is one LSTM layer with 32 hidden units. It is drawn once per hour only to show time passing; all the boxes are the same layer with the same weights. At every hour it reads that hour's 5 input values and passes two things to the next hour: its long-term memory (c) and its hidden state (h). The LSTM also produces an output at every hour, but we only use the one after the last hour (48): by then the hidden state summarizes the whole window. A single linear layer turns those 32 numbers into one forecast, 6 hours ahead.

Train Model trains a new LSTM with the settings above; Load Pre-trained loads one trained longer beforehand (shown when the notebook opens).
Train Model starts from random weights and uses the target, history, horizon and input variables chosen in Step 2. Load Pre-trained loads an LSTM trained beforehand for 40 epochs with fixed settings: temperature, 48 hours of history, 6 hours ahead, inputs temperature, humidity and rainfall, 32 hidden units. When it is loaded, the results below use those settings.
Results for the pre-trained LSTM (40 epochs; temperature, 48 h history, 6 h ahead)

• The learning curve shows the average error on the training and validation periods after each epoch. The dotted line is the "same hour yesterday" baseline on the validation period: the LSTM is only useful once its validation curve drops below it.
  • The bar chart compares all three on the test period, which was never used during training.
  • Try a horizon of 1 hour and of 24 hours. When does the LSTM help most?

Step 5: Predictions and where they fail

History, what really happened, and each forecast for one test example.
The gray line on the left is the input the network read. The dashed line is what really happened afterwards; the black dot is the true value F hours ahead. The green star is the LSTM's forecast, and the square and diamond are the two baselines. Turn on Show the worst prediction to see the test example with the largest LSTM error: these are often sudden changes, such as a cold rainy afternoon, that the past hours did not announce.

Look inside: the hidden state

Some hidden units of the trained LSTM, read hour by hour over three days.
We feed three days of weather into the trained network and record its hidden state after every hour. We show the units whose values follow the input series most closely. Many of them rise and fall with the daily cycle, even though nobody told the network that days exist: it learned that this rhythm is useful for forecasting. This is the RNN version of the learned filters we saw in the CNN.

Coffee leaf rust spreads when leaves stay wet and temperatures are mild, so a forecast of humid hours a day ahead can tell a farmer when to inspect or protect plants (the orchestration example from Session 1). The same window → forecast recipe works for soil moisture, river levels or greenhouse sensors: only the input columns change.

data.text/markdown:
What to notice

  • An RNN reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a hidden state forward; the same weights are reused at every step.
  • An LSTM adds gates that decide what to remember, so it can use information from many hours back.
  • A forecast is only useful if it beats simple baselines such as persistence and "same hour yesterday".

Questions for discussion

  1. Does a longer history always help? Try 24 hours and 120 hours.
  2. When does the LSTM beat the baselines by the most: 1 hour ahead or 24 hours ahead? Why?
